core: A stack is a LIFO (last-in, first-out) collection: only the most recently added item can be removed next
The core operations push (add to top), pop (remove and return top), peek/top (read top without removing), and isEmpty
Each core operation is O(1) time when the stack is implemented on a dynamic array or a linked list
Overflow (pushing onto a full fixed-capacity stack) and underflow (popping or peeking an empty stack) as the two error conditions
Real uses: the call stack for function calls, undo/redo, expression evaluation, balanced-bracket matching, and depth-first search (DFS)
Two small Bash-verified worked examples: push 1,2,3 then pop returns 3,2,1; and balanced-bracket matching of a string
supporting: A stack is an abstract data type (ADT): it is defined by its LIFO behaviour and operations, not by any one implementation
A stack can be implemented on top of an array/dynamic array or a linked list; the implementation is named, not re-taught here
One contrast sentence with the queue (FIFO), whose operations belong to the sibling queues topic
outOfScope: Queues and FIFO enqueue/dequeue operations (own sibling topic: queues)
How dynamic arrays and linked lists work internally (own sibling topics: arrays, lists)
Recursion mechanics and base cases beyond noting that recursion runs on the call stack (own sibling topic: recursion)
Full expression-evaluation and DFS algorithms (named as uses only, not taught in full)

claims.claim: A stack is a collection in which only the most recently added item may be removed; the latest added item is at the top, and the discipline is last-in, first-out (LIFO).
The basic stack operations are push (add an item to the top) and pop (remove the most recently added item); top/peek (read the top item) and isEmpty are commonly available as well.

When a stack is backed by a dynamic array, push is add(n, x) and pop is remove(n-1), operating only at the end of the sequence; these top-only operations run in O(1) time (amortized for a dynamic array).
claims.verification: Definition of push/pop as operations at the end of an ArrayStack confirmed against Open Data Structures; the LIFO order and O(1)-at-the-top behaviour were also reproduced in Python 3.9.6 via Bash on 2026-08-19.

claims.claim: In Python a list can be used directly as a stack: append() pushes to the top and pop() without an index removes and returns the top, giving last-in, first-out order.
claims.verification: Executed in Python 3.9.6 via Bash on 2026-08-19: pushing 1,2,3 with append then calling pop three times returned 3,2,1.

claims.claim: Pushing three values 1, 2, 3 onto an empty stack and then popping twice returns 3 then 2 and leaves 1 on the stack.
claims.verification: Traced and executed in Python 3.9.6 via Bash on 2026-08-19; pop order was [3, 2] with [1] remaining.

claims.claim: Balanced-bracket matching can be decided with a stack: push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket pop and check that it matches the expected opener; the string is balanced only if every pop matches and the stack is empty at the end. The string '([)]' is unbalanced because when ')' is read the popped bracket is '[', which does not match.
claims.verification: Implemented and executed in Python 3.9.6 via Bash on 2026-08-19 across cases including '([]{})' (balanced), '{[()]}' (balanced), '(]' , '(()' , ')(' , and '([)]' (all unbalanced); results matched the described rule.

claims.claim: The mechanism that tracks active function calls is the call stack: the most recently called function is the first to finish and return, which is LIFO order; recursion relies on this call stack.
A stack (LIFO) differs from a queue (FIFO): a stack removes the most recently added item, while a queue removes the oldest.

Supports the definition, the operations, and the LIFO framing. Prose synthesized, not copied.

Used for the concrete Python implementation and to verify the push 1,2,3 -> pop 3,2,1 trace. Prose original.
